questions.prompt: DESIGN IT — [senior] nested folder sharing, public links and a shared-with-me view at scale (organized-study-linkwarden, linkwarden/fabledocs/upskill/03-architecture-and-patterns/03-validation-auth-and-permissions.md). Scenario: two years on the service has 400,000 users and 900,000 collections, nested up to eight levels deep. A design agency wants to share one client's folder tree (a sub-collection with 60 descendants) with 12 client contacts who must see that subtree and nothing above or beside it; marketing wants per-link share URLs that expire after a week; a consultant who belongs to 1,500 collections waits 9 seconds for the list of collections shared with her; and last month an owner deleted a parent folder and 40 sub-collections created by other members went with it. Write your design before you look: how rights flow down a tree and how a check reads them, how a subtree is shared with outsiders, what a public or share URL identifies and how it is revoked or expires, how the shared-with-me list is served for someone in 1,500 collections, what deleting or moving a folder does to what other people created inside it, and what a public page reveals about the people in a collection. Then tick the checkpoints you covered and add up the weights (suggested pass: 70% with every [w3] hit)

keyPoints.text: [w3] Inherit at read, from an indexed ancestry: the only ancestry walk today, run when a sub-collection is created, climbs the parent chain one query per level, so reusing it for every inherited check would cost eight round trips at eight levels; store each collection's ancestor ids (a closure table or materialized path) so 'may this user read it' is one indexed query over memberships on the collection or any ancestor.

[w3] Rights flow down, never up or sideways: the client contacts get membership rows on the shared subtree's root only, which reach its descendants through inheritance; nothing gives them its ancestors or siblings, while members of the agency's higher folders still see the subtree from above. The current check reads only direct membership on the one collection asked about, so this is a new rule, not a tweak.

[w3] A share URL names a token, not a row: today 'public' is a flag on a collection served by its auto-incrementing integer id, so every public collection can be found by counting upward. Share links become rows of their own (random token, scope of one link or one subtree, expiry, creator, revoked-at), the URL carries only the token, and revoking or expiring the row ends access at once.

[w2] A public page should not publish the people: the public collection response today includes every member's username, display name and picture, so an anonymous visitor learns who works in the team; return the links and an owner-chosen display name, nothing more.

[w3] The 9-second list is one unpaginated query that returns every owned or joined collection with each one's full member list and user details: 1,500 collections at about 30 members each is some 45,000 member rows for one page load. Page it, return member counts instead of members, and fetch a collection's members only when it is opened.

[w2] The membership table is keyed user-first and its only extra index is on the user again, so listing a collection's members, or checking a whole ancestry for one user, has no collection-led index to use; add an index led by the collection id before building inheritance on top of it.

[w3] Deleting a parent deletes everything under it: the delete walks every sub-collection and removes its members, links, search entries and archive folders (the schema cascades the same way), so one owner's delete removed work other members created. Make deletion a soft delete with a restore window, list what will go (and who created it) before confirming, and offer to move other people's sub-collections out first.

[w1] Keep the two revocation levers visibly apart: removing a member is a membership change, while killing a share URL is a token revocation, and neither is the same as revoking a login, since sessions and API keys live in one token table.
keyPoints.quote: Session tokens and API keys share the `AccessToken` table

questions.prompt: PRE-MORTEM — the nested-sharing release has been out for a month. A client contact notices the names of other clients' folders in her sidebar; an owner drags the shared client folder under a different parent and the 12 contacts suddenly see a sibling folder full of internal notes; a contact removed from the client folder can still open a deep sub-folder an hour later; a scraper harvests 12,000 public collections and their members' names over a weekend; and one owner's attempt to re-parent a folder hangs a server process. What breaks, how does each show up, and what in your design prevents it?

keyPoints.text: [w3] The sidebar leaks parent names: the collections list returns, for each collection, its parent's id and name, so a member of only a sub-collection learns what the folder above it is called. Under subtree sharing, return a parent only when the caller may read it, and show the shared root as a top-level entry for outsiders.

[w3] Moving a folder is a permission change: under inheritance its audience becomes whoever can read the new parent, so a move must show who gains and loses access before it is confirmed, and today only the owner of both the folder and the new parent may move it, a check worth keeping.

[w3] Stale inherited access is a cache problem: if effective rights per user and collection are precomputed, a removal must invalidate them for the whole subtree in the same change, or the check must read memberships and ancestry live. A one-hour lag means rights were cached with a timeout and no invalidation.

[w2] The harvest needed nothing clever: sequential ids plus a public flag make every public collection reachable by counting, and each response lists members. Random tokens, no member data on public pages and rate limits on the public routes close it; logging public hits per collection shows the scan.

[w3] The hang is a cycle: the re-parent check compares the new parent's own parent with the new parent id instead of with the folder being moved, so making a folder a child of its own descendant (or of itself) passes; the ancestor walk used when creating sub-collections then loops with no visited set, and the walk behind apply-to-sub-collections tracks seen ids but still feeds every child back into its frontier, so the next propagating save on that folder spins too. Refuse any move whose new parent has the folder among its ancestors, and give every tree walk a visited set and a depth cap.

questions.prompt: TRADE-OFF HANDBACK — defend your nested-sharing design against the alternatives: inheriting rights at read time versus copying member rows down the tree versus per-object grants; a public flag versus random share tokens versus signed expiring URLs; cascading deletes versus soft deletes versus re-homing other people's children; embedding members in the collections list versus paging with counts; and a closure table versus a materialized path versus a recursive query at read time. For each, say what you bought and what it cost.

keyPoints.text: [w3] Inheriting at read keeps one source of truth and makes a removal effective everywhere below at once, at the cost of an ancestry lookup on every check; copying rows down (the existing apply-to-sub-collections save) deletes every descendant's member rows and recreates them from the parent's list, so a contact added to one sub-folder only is silently dropped on the next save, and 12 contacts on a 61-folder subtree is 732 rows rewritten per change; per-object grants allow exceptions such as one hidden sub-folder, at the cost of rules users struggle to predict.

[w3] A public flag needs no table but, on integer ids, is found by counting, and each public collection's links are fetchable by their own ids; a share token scoped to a subtree must be resolved against the ancestry on every request and checked for expiry and revocation, at the cost of a lookup per view and a management screen; a per-link token avoids the ancestry lookup but cannot follow a folder's growth.

[w2] Cascades keep the data model simple and leave no orphans, at the price of one person destroying others' work; soft delete adds a restore window and a filter on every read; re-homing other people's sub-collections respects their work but surprises the owner and needs a rule for where they go.

[w2] Embedding members makes the sidebar a single request and is fine for a handful of collections; paging with counts keeps the list fast at 1,500 memberships and stops shipping everyone's names to every client, at the cost of extra requests when a collection is opened.

[w2] A closure table answers ancestry with one indexed join and handles moves as a bounded rewrite of the moved subtree's rows; a materialized path is one column and fast prefix matches, but every move rewrites the path of every descendant; a recursive query needs no extra storage but repeats the walk on every check, which is the cost the current code already pays one level at a time.
